7 Mic + one FOH question list (Ch. 30–31). Run the song once live-like.

| 8 | Short set (two songs). Cool-down. Review CSV. Do not add distortion this week unless the cut requires it and Ch. 10 is clean.

If a week leaves you hoarse, that week failed. Repeat it easier, do not “push through.”

35 · Close

Method: instrument, short daily work, a song map, then the room.

Tools: warm-up generator (Ch. 6), genre routines (Ch. 7), mapper table (Ch. 14), CSV, TTS in the shell. No keys in the files.

Stop rule still wins.

If you change the outline later, keep Ch. 14. The three demos can move. The template cannot.

36 · Glossary

Terms as this book uses them. Plain English, one idea per entry. Nothing here diagnoses a voice — persistent hoarseness, pain, missing notes, or effortful talking mean see an otolaryngologist.

Terms

Abduction. The opening of the vocal folds, moving the arytenoids apart so air can pass. Breathing in requires it; voicing needs the folds to come back together afterward.

Adduction. The closing of the vocal folds so their edges meet and vibrate. Good adduction is a light, complete seal, not a squeeze.

Alignment. The stacking of head, ribcage, and pelvis so breath and larynx work without fighting the posture. It is a moving balance, not a locked stance.

Allergens. Airborne irritants such as dust, pollen, mold, and dander that inflame the nose and throat and can mimic a vocal problem. Treat the allergy before blaming technique.

Appoggio. The Italian term for “lean”: after inhaling, the sternum and ribcage stay buoyant so the diaphragm’s passive rise is slowed. The diaphragm is an inspiratory muscle and stays largely passive during phonation.

Aryepiglottic sphincter. The ring formed by the arytenoids and the epiglottis at the top of the larynx. Narrowing it focuses the sound and is the main structure behind twang.

Arytenoid. A pair of small cartilages at the back of the larynx that open and close the vocal folds. Most pitch and closure adjustments involve them.

Aspiration. A small leak of air through the folds, heard as an “h” within or before a note. A little is a breathy onset; a lot is inefficient and rough on the voice.

Back-phrasing. Singing a phrase deliberately behind the beat for a relaxed, conversational feel. Common in jazz and R&B.

Bel canto. The Italian “beautiful singing” tradition that prizes even tone, smooth register transitions, and legato across the range. It assumes appoggio and a quiet, efficient onset.

Belt. A loud, speech-like chest-voice sound carried high in the range with firm fold closure and a bright vowel. It is a coordination, not simply volume.

Breath management. The skill of spending air efficiently across a phrase so closure and pressure stay steady. It is the practical replacement for the vague instruction to “support.”

Breath map. A written plan of where each phrase in a song will take its breath. It turns breathing from an emergency into a decision.

Breath support. The coordinated control of airflow and pressure that keeps the folds meeting steadily. In practice it means steady pressure from below, not pushing or holding.

Breathiness. Audible air escaping past the folds because closure is incomplete. It can be a style choice or a sign of weakness or swelling.

Chest voice. The speaking-range sound made with the vocal folds shortened and thickened. It is the same family as belt and M1.

Chiaro. Italian for “bright”: the forward, ringing quality produced by a narrowed epilaryngeal tube and strong higher-formant energy. Bright helps a voice cut.

Chiaroscuro. Italian for “bright-dark”: the classical ideal of pairing a ringing bright core with a warm, rounded body. It is a balance, not two separate colors.

Closed quotient. The fraction of each vibration cycle the vocal folds stay in contact. Higher closure (chest, belt) sounds full and pressed; lower closure (falsetto) sounds lighter.

Compression. In the voice, the firm but healthy meeting of the fold edges under pressure. Closure and breath energy create it; squeezing the throat does not.

Compression (audio). A studio tool that narrows a signal’s loudest and quietest parts toward each other. It evens a vocal in a mix but does not fix technique.

Cool-down. Gentle humming or a speech-range glide after singing to ease the voice down from high load. It is a comfort measure, not a proven repair for a wrecked set.

Copertura. Italian for “covered”: a vowel darkened and rounded toward an “oh” as pitch rises, keeping the vibratory mode consistent up the scale. It is a classical way to avoid shouting.

Cricothyroid (CT). The muscle that tilts the thyroid cartilage forward and stretches the vocal folds thin. CT-dominant singing is head voice, falsetto, and M2.

Cry. A slightly whiny, pleading quality that nudges the folds toward better closure and a warmer tone. It is common in musical theatre and sob-adjacent pop.

Cupping. Holding a hand over the microphone head, which traps air and muddies the sound while raising feedback risk. Do not do it.

Diaphragm. The dome-shaped muscle under the lungs that does most of the work of inhaling. It is an inspiratory muscle and relaxes upward during singing; you do not push air out with it.

Epiglottis. The leaf-shaped cartilage above the folds that folds down over the airway when you swallow. It also helps shape the small resonating space just above the larynx.

Epilaryngeal tube. The short, narrow resonant chamber just above the vocal folds, formed by the aryepiglottic structures. Tightening it raises high-formant energy and produces ring and twang.

Fach. The German system for classifying opera roles by voice range, weight, and color (lyric, dramatic, coloratura, and so on). It matters for casting, not for pop or musical theatre.

Falsetto. A light register made with thin, stretched folds that do not fully close, so some air escapes. In men it sits above the speaking range; in women it overlaps head voice and is often called M2.

Feedback. The squeal that happens when a microphone picks up sound coming back out of a speaker and re-amplifies it. Managing it is about mic position, monitor level, and EQ, not singing louder.

FOH. “Front of house”: the engineer and mixing position facing the stage, controlling what the audience hears. Your monitor is what you hear; FOH is what they hear.

Formant (F1, F2). A resonance of the vocal tract that makes certain harmonics loud and shapes which vowel you hear. F1 tracks tongue height and mouth opening; F2 tracks how far forward the tongue is.

Formant tuning. Adjusting the tract so a resonance lines up with a harmonic of the note being sung, boosting it. It is how singers get loud and clear without more effort.

Forward placement. A sensation of buzz or ring near the front of the face when the tract is tuned well. The feeling is real, but the sound comes from the whole filter, not from a cavity in the mask.

Gain. The amount of amplification applied to an input or signal. Set it with headroom in mind; more gain is not more presence.

Glottal stop/onset. A sound made by fully closing the folds and then releasing them, like the catch in “uh-oh.” As a stylistic onset it is punchy; as a habit it is a hard, wearing way to start every note.

Glottis. The opening between the vocal folds. Its closing creates voice; its opening lets air pass.

Grit. A rough, rasping texture produced by the false folds or other supraglottic structures over a still-clear pitch. It is an effect layered on the note, not damage to the true folds.

Growl. A low, rattling distortion made mainly by engaging the arytenoid cartilages or epiglottis over a steady pitch. Like grit, it sits over a still-periodic true-fold tone.

Hard onset. Starting a note with a firm slam of the folds, often with a glottal stop. Fine occasionally for effect, but habitual hard onsets press and tire the voice.

Head voice. The lighter, higher register made with stretched, thinned folds. It overlaps with falsetto and M2.

HPF. High-pass filter: an EQ setting that cuts low frequencies, removing rumble, handling noise, and proximity boom. A standard starting point on a vocal channel.

Humidity. The amount of water vapor in the air, which affects how well the vocal folds stay lubricated. Dry air dries the throat; adding moisture to the room helps.

Hydration. Drinking water to keep the body and the thin mucus layer over the folds lubricated. Systemic hydration helps; gargling does little.

Hyoid. The small U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue, above the larynx, anchoring many muscles of the tongue and throat. Its height shapes both the vowel and the quality.

IEM. In-ear monitor: a molded or generic earphone that feeds your own mix directly to your ears. It replaces a floor monitor and can stop you from over-singing to hear yourself.

Inhalation phonation. Voicing while air flows in, used in therapy for muscle tension problems. It is a tool, not a performance sound.

Intercostals. The muscles between the ribs that raise and lower the ribcage. They help keep the ribs buoyant during the slow exhale of singing.

Laryngeal height. How high or low the larynx sits in the throat, which changes the length and shape of the tract. A neutral-to-slightly-low larynx gives a rounder classical color; a higher one gives a brighter, speech-like pop color.

Laryngeal tilt. The forward rocking of the thyroid cartilage that stretches the folds, driven by the cricothyroid. More tilt means higher pitch and a thinner fold shape.

Laryngoscopy. A doctor’s exam of the larynx, usually with a tiny camera, to see the folds directly. It is the standard way to check for swelling, nodules, or other problems.

Larynx. The voice box in the front of the neck, housing the vocal folds and the cartilages that move them. It both protects the airway and makes sound.

LEDE. “Live end, dead end”: a room design that absorbs early reflections near the speakers and lets the rear of the room stay reflective. It is a studio and rehearsal-room idea, not a stage setup.

Legato. Smooth, connected singing with no gaps between notes. It depends on steady airflow and even fold closure.

Lip trill. A semi-occluded warm-up in which you blow through relaxed, fluttering lips on a pitch. The back-pressure helps the folds meet without pushing.

M1. The register of the lower and middle range where the folds are short and thick and close firmly. It is the acoustic name for chest voice and belt.

M2. The higher register where the folds are stretched thin and closure is lighter. It is the acoustic name for head voice and falsetto.

Mask resonance. The buzz felt around the nose and cheekbones when the tract is tuned well and the sound is forward. It is a sensation, not a separate resonator you sing into.

Messa di voce. A single sustained note swelled from soft to loud and back to soft. It trains steady breath and even registration and is a classic test of control.

Mic proximity. How close the mouth is to the microphone, which changes both loudness and tone. Closer is fuller and boomier; pulling back is cleaner and thinner.

Mic technique. Using distance and angle to control level, tone, and feedback while you sing. It is a skill as real as breath control.

Mix. A weighted coordination between the thick-fold and thin-fold actions, blending chest and head rather than switching between them. It is not a third register.

Modal register. The everyday speaking-range register, with the folds in their normal thick vibratory mode. It is the same family as chest voice and M1.

Monitor. A speaker or earphone that sends sound back to the performer. What you hear on stage is the monitor; what the crowd hears is front of house.

Muscle tension dysphonia. A voice problem caused by excessive or mistimed muscle effort around the larynx rather than by the folds themselves. It often responds to therapy and better coordination, not rest alone.

Nasality. Sound escaping through the nose because the soft palate does not seal the nasal passage. A little can brighten a pop tone; too much makes vowels honky and unclear.

Nasendoscopy. A doctor’s exam using a thin flexible scope passed through the nose to view the larynx and folds. It is common when a voice problem needs a closer look.

Obliques. The muscles along the sides of the abdomen that help control the exhale and stabilize the trunk. They assist breath management but do not push the voice.

Off-axis. Placing or pointing a microphone away from the direct line of the mouth to reduce boom, plosives, and sibilance. It is a standard way to tame a loud source.

Onsets. How a note begins: the moment the folds come together and air starts the sound. Clean onsets set up every phrase that follows.

Ossia / speech vowel. “Ossia” means “or”: an alternate vowel or note offered in place of the written one, usually to keep a high passage singable. The substitute is often a slightly modified version of the plain speech vowel.

Passaggio. Italian for “passage”: the zone where registration shifts, as the fold adjustment changes near the top of the speaking range. Managing it well means blending, not avoiding it.

Performance load. The total demand a show puts on your voice: range, volume, duration, and how often. Know it before you agree to it.

Phonation. The act of the vocal folds vibrating to make voiced sound. It begins with the folds closing against the airflow.

Phrasing. Shaping a line of a song: where it breathes, where it pushes, where it eases. Good phrasing serves the lyric first.

Pitch. How high or low a note sounds, set by how fast the vocal folds vibrate. Faster vibration is higher; slower is lower.

Placement. Where the sound seems to sit — forward, back, in the mask — when the tract is shaped a certain way. It is a feel that follows resonance, not a place you put the tone.

Posture. How you hold the whole body while singing, which sets up the breath and larynx. Balanced posture lets the ribs move freely instead of collapsing.

Presbyphonia. The gradual weakening and thinning of the voice with age. It is common and often responds well to training and therapy.

Pressed phonation. Using too much closure and pressure so the folds grind together. It is the wear pattern behind most vocal injury, not a technique.

Projection. Being heard across a room without a microphone. It comes from resonance and tuning, not from shouting.

Proximity effect. The boost in low frequencies that happens when a source gets very close to a directional microphone. It makes voices sound warmer and fuller up close.

Puberphonia. A voice disorder in which a young man’s voice stays high and childlike after puberty. It is treatable with therapy.

Reflux/GERD. Stomach acid backing up into the throat, which irritates the folds and can cause hoarseness, a lump feeling, and morning voice problems. Manage it with diet, timing, and medical advice.

Register. A set of pitches produced with a similar fold adjustment and sound quality. Chest and head are the two main families.

Registration. How smoothly you move between registers. Good registration hides the seams rather than eliminating the registers.

Resonance. The boosting of certain frequencies by the vocal tract. It is what makes a vowel and what lets a voice carry.

Rest. Time for the voice to recover from load, which is often the only real fix for fatigue. Silent recovery matters as much as technique.

Retroflex. A tongue shape with the tip curled back, which lowers one of the higher resonances and can darken or cover the tone. It is a subtle color tool, not a default vowel.

Reverb. Simulated or real reflections that make a voice sound like it is in a space. It can flatter a voice or hide its problems; mix with care.

Ribcage. The basket of ribs around the lungs. Keeping it buoyant after the inhale is the physical core of appoggio.

Sibilant. A hissing consonant such as “s,” “sh,” or “z,” made by forcing air through a narrow channel. They carry no pitch and can spike a recording.

Singer's formant. A cluster of boosted energy around 3 kHz formed by F3–F5. It lets an unamplified voice cut through an orchestra in a frequency band where the instruments are weak.

Sostenuto. Italian for “sustained”: a steady, even held tone with no wobble or fade. It is a test of breath and control.

Sotto voce. Italian for “under the voice”: singing quietly and intimately, close to a whisper. It takes more control than it sounds.

Soundcheck. The pre-show run-through where levels, monitors, and mics are set. Use it to solve problems before the audience is in the room.

SOVT. Semi-occluded vocal tract: exercises such as lip trills, straw phonation, and voiced “ng” or “m.” The partial narrowing creates back-pressure so the folds meet with less pushing.

Speech-level singing. A method that keeps the laryngeal adjustment and vowel shapes close to speech across the range. It aims for a light, consistent through-line rather than a big register shift.

Staccato. Notes sung short and separated, the opposite of legato. It relies on quick, clean onsets.

Sternum. The breastbone in the center of the chest, which stays lifted and buoyant in appoggio. Its height is a useful checkpoint for the ribcage.

Strain. The feeling of effort or squeeze in the throat or neck while singing. It is a warning sign, not a badge of work.

Straw phonation. A semi-occluded exercise in which you sing or hum through a narrow straw. The back-pressure helps the folds meet with less effort.

Subglottal pressure. The air pressure below the vocal folds that drives them into vibration. Singing needs steady, moderate pressure, not a maximum.

Support. The coordinated breath control that keeps subglottal pressure steady so the folds can work efficiently. It is steady management, not a push.

Tessitura. The pitch range where a song mostly sits, which can be narrow even in a wide-ranging song. A comfortable tessitura matters more than hitting one high note.

Thyroarytenoid (TA). The muscle inside the vocal folds that shortens and thickens them. TA-dominant singing is chest voice, belt, and M1.

Timbre. The color or character of a voice, set by its harmonic content. It is why two singers on the same note sound different.

Tongue root. The back of the tongue, whose tension can pull the larynx up and darken or tense the tone. Keeping it relaxed helps a free sound.

Tongue trill. A semi-occluded warm-up where the tongue tip trills, like a rolled “r.” It gives back-pressure and frees the jaw and tongue.

Trachea. The windpipe below the larynx that carries air to and from the lungs. Subglottal pressure is measured in this tube.

Transverse abdominis. The deep abdominal muscle that wraps the lower trunk and helps stabilize the exhale. It supports breath management without pushing the voice.

Twang. A bright, buzzy resonance made by narrowing the epilaryngeal tube. It is the narrowness that gives many pop and belt voices their edge.

Ventricular folds. The “false” folds just above the true vocal folds. They normally stay out of the way, but they create grit and distortion when they engage.

Vibrato. A regular, even oscillation in pitch and loudness on a sustained note, usually about five to seven cycles per second. It is a sign of a free, balanced voice.

Vocal folds. The two bands of tissue in the larynx that vibrate to make voice. They come together, stretch, and thin to change pitch and quality.

Vocal fry. A low, crackly register made with slow, irregular fold vibration and very little pitch. It can be a style choice, but leaning on it at the bottom of the range can tire the voice.

Vocal hemorrhage. Bleeding into the vocal fold tissue from forceful use, causing sudden hoarseness and loss of range. It is a medical emergency for a singer: stop singing and see a doctor.

Vocal hygiene. The habits that protect the voice: hydration, rest, load management, and avoiding irritants and shouting. It is the daily-care side of training.

Vocal load. The total amount of voice use, including talking, singing, and shouting. Tracking it is how you avoid stacking fatigue on top of training.

Vocal nap. A short period of deliberate silence to let a tired voice recover. Twenty minutes of not talking can do more than another exercise.

Vocal nodules. Small callus-like growths on the fold edges from repeated collision and pressure. They cause hoarseness and usually need rest, therapy, and a look at technique.

Vocal tract. The tube of throat, mouth, and nose above the vocal folds that filters the sound into vowels and timbre. Its shape, not the folds, decides most of the color.

Voicing. Whether a sound is voiced (folds vibrating) or unvoiced (just air). Vowels are voiced; “s” and “f” are not.

Volume. How loud a sound is, which in singing comes from air pressure and closure working together. It is not the same as effort.

Vowel modification. Adjusting a vowel, usually more open on high notes, so the tract keeps resonating well up the range. It is a deliberate change, not a mistake.

Warm-up. A short, gentle sequence that reminds breath, folds, and tract how to work together for the range you will sing. It is mostly skill re-acquisition, not a magic change in the tissue.

Wedge. A floor monitor angled up at the performer so they can hear themselves. It is the alternative to an in-ear monitor.

Whistle register. The highest register, above M2, made with a tiny, mostly closed opening of the folds. It produces a thin, flute-like sound.

Y-buzz. A semi-occluded exercise on a “y” sound, as in “yes,” that keeps the tongue high and the tract narrow. It encourages forward resonance and easy closure.

Vowel symbols

These are the vowel symbols used in this book, with a familiar example word.

Symbol Example word
ɑ father
æ cat
ɔ thought
ɪ sit
ʌ strut
ə about
u boot
o more
e bet
i see
aɪ sky
eɪ say
oʊ go
aʊ now
ɔɪ boy

The first two formants do the work. F1 rises as the mouth opens and the tongue lowers (as in ɑ and æ), and F2 rises as the tongue moves forward (as in i and e) and falls as it moves back (as in u and o). Singers retune these two resonances on high notes so the vowel stays recognizable while the tone stays strong.

Abbreviations

TA. Thyroarytenoid — the muscle that shortens and thickens the folds; the chest/belt/M1 side of registration.

CT. Cricothyroid — the muscle that stretches and thins the folds; the head/falsetto/M2 side of registration.

SOVT. Semi-occluded vocal tract — exercises with a partial narrowing, such as lip trills and straw phonation.

CCM. Contemporary Commercial Music — pop, rock, R&B, country, musical theatre, and other non-classical styles.

MT. Musical theatre — the stage genre with its own mix of speech-like singing and belt.

FOH. Front of house — the mixing position and the sound the audience hears.

HPF. High-pass filter — an EQ setting that cuts low frequencies to remove rumble and boom.

IEM. In-ear monitor — an earphone that feeds the performer their own mix.

ENT. Ear, nose, and throat specialist — the doctor who examines and treats the larynx.

SLP. Speech-language pathologist — the clinician who works on voice disorders and retraining.

SPL. Sound pressure level — the measured loudness of a sound, in decibels.

DAW. Digital audio workstation — the software used to record, edit, and mix audio.

EQ. Equalizer — a tool for boosting or cutting specific frequency ranges.

dB. Decibel — the unit used to measure loudness.

Hz. Hertz — cycles per second; the unit of frequency and pitch.

kHz. Kilohertz — one thousand hertz.

f0. The fundamental frequency — the rate at which the folds vibrate, which we hear as the pitch.

F1/F2. The first and second formants — the two tract resonances that define a vowel.

M1/M2. The two main registers: M1 for the thicker lower coordination, M2 for the thinner upper one.

CQ. Closed quotient — the portion of each cycle the folds stay closed.

Psub. Subglottal pressure — the air pressure below the folds that drives them into vibration.

SAID. Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands — you get the coordination you train, which is why classical-only practice does not build belt.

GERD. Gastroesophageal reflux disease — acid backing up into the throat, a common cause of morning hoarseness.

VOC. Volatile organic compounds — airborne chemicals from paint, cleaners, and new materials that can irritate the vocal folds.

PA. Public address system — the speakers and amplification that carry the voice to the audience.

37 · Voice teachers on YouTube

Every channel below is a free library, not a replacement for a teacher who can hear you in a room. Use them to copy an exercise, follow a warm-up, or hear a concept explained a second way. Where a channel is easier to find by name than by a guessed link, the search phrase is given instead of an address.

Foundations & warm-ups

Eric Arceneaux (AApproach) — https://www.youtube.com/user/EricArceneaux — A long-running catalog of vocal workouts, warm-ups, and breath-control drills, with steady attention to protecting the voice between shows. Good for singers who want short, repeatable routines rather than one-off tips.

Jeff Rolka — search "Jeff Rolka warm up" — Long follow-along warm-ups with almost no talking, built to run from the bottom to the top of the range. The gentle, all-voices routines suit anyone who wants to warm up without being coached mid-exercise.

Ramsey Voice Studio — search "Ramsey Voice Studio professional vocal warm up" — A structured daily routine with separate scale sets for men and women. Watch when you want an ordered session you can repeat on the same days each week.

30 Day Singer — https://www.youtube.com/c/30DaySinger — Beginner-friendly courses and short daily exercises. Best for someone new to training who wants a clear starting sequence.

Jacob's Vocal Academy — https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCmHvG9kF8TYF50W5JW-J8wQ — Scales and exercises with backing tracks, so you can practice in tune without a keyboard in front of you.

Freya Casey — search "Freya Casey singing" — Warm-ups and beginner-friendly lessons, explained plainly. A good first stop if the pace of a bigger tutorial channel goes by too fast.

Healthy Vocal Technique (Victoria) — search "Healthy Vocal Technique" — Practical, no-nonsense technique videos on keeping the voice working. A calm counterweight to channels built on big demonstrations.

Classical & opera

Claire Galloway — search "Claire Galloway Technique Tuesday" — A classical technique series that works through breath, resonance, and vowels one step at a time. Useful for the singer moving from pop habits toward an unamplified, legato sound.

Rachel Willis-Sorensen — search "Rachel Willis-Sorensen Warmup Wednesday" — Opera warm-ups and technical talk from a working professional. Worth watching to see how a full-time opera singer maintains and builds a voice, not just exercises in isolation.

Contemporary, rock & distortion

Ken Tamplin Vocal Academy — https://www.youtube.com/user/kentamplin — Rock and pop belting, vocal strength, and range-building. Aimed at singers who want power and stamina; treat the heaviest demonstrations as goals to work toward, not to copy at full volume on day one.

Chris Liepe — https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCatVlK-imF7H9o0RDGOYWAg — Contemporary and rock technique with a real interest in breath and support mechanics, and distortion explored with care rather than as a party trick. The channel to pair with Ch. 10 if you want clean-tone-first grit explained.

Tara Simon Studios — search "Tara Simon Studios" — Contemporary technique tutorials and song breakdowns, pitched at working and aspiring pop singers.

Felicia Ricci — https://www.youtube.com/user/booklovin — Tension release, high notes, mic technique, and singing with emotion. A good bridge between technique and performance for theatre and pop singers.

Musical theatre

Natalie Weiss — search "Natalie Weiss Breaking Down the Riffs" — Musical theatre riffing and coaching sessions. Watch to hear how a working Broadway singer shapes runs and draws honest ranges out of students.

The Songbird Tree (Kerri Ho) — search "The Songbird Tree Kerri Ho musical theatre" — Mix and belt for musical theatre. Useful when you are sorting legit, mix, and belt into separate coordinations (Ch. 12) instead of one blended "theatre sound."

The Musical Theatre Coach (Karen Souza) — search "Karen Souza musical theatre warm ups" — A seven-minute daily musical theatre warm-up you can actually finish before a show. Practical when time is short.

Tina's Vocal Studio — search "Tina's Vocal Studio belting" — Belt technique for Broadway and pop. Watch for the belt-first approach; keep a clean tone before adding belt color.

Pedagogy & anatomy

New York Vocal Coaching (Justin Stoney) — https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcxo5COqhVc84JYS_bRdLyg — The "Voice Lessons To The World" library, one topic per video, covering breath, style, and audition nerves. The closest thing online to a free, well-organized curriculum, and a good reference when you meet a term you do not know.

SingWise Vocal Training (Karyn O'Connor) — https://www.youtube.com/@singwisevocals — Anatomy-led pedagogy rather than buzzwords. Watch when you want to know what is actually moving, and why "support" is not one muscle.

Dr. Dan's Voice Essentials — https://www.youtube.com/c/DrDansVoiceEssentials — Healthy habits, warm-ups, and performance tips, delivered by a voice scientist. Good for grounding Ch. 33 in something more than folklore.

Andy Follin — search "Andy Follin vocal coach" — Estill-informed, evidence-leaning explanations of what the folds and the vocal tract are doing. Useful when a word like "twang" or "cry" needs an operational definition.

A caveat before you binge

Approaches differ, and they conflict. Some of the most popular channels teach a version of "diaphragm support" — air driven from the belly, or pushing down on the diaphragm. This book treats the diaphragm differently: it is an inspiratory muscle, largely passive while you sing, and real support is appoggio — a buoyant sternum and ribcage with a metered exhalation (Ch. 2). You can still take the warm-ups and the exercises; just translate the language. The part you can actually feel and train — ribs staying up, the sideways breath, a steady release — is the same whatever the label.

Two rules carry over from the rest of the book. Keep the stop rule: pain, lasting hoarseness, or a sudden loss of range is a reason to see a physician, not to try another exercise. And no channel can hear you, so use these to fill the gaps between lessons rather than to replace a teacher who can tell you what you are actually doing.

38 · Further reading

A short shelf for going deeper than a channel or a lesson can take you. These are working references, not endorsements; read the ones that match the question in front of you. Where a book is heavier than you need, the journals and organizations at the end are the faster route.

Voice science & acoustics

  • The Science of the Singing Voice — Johan Sundberg — The standard account of the acoustics and physiology of singing; read it for the source-filter model and formant behavior in plain technical prose.
  • Principles of Voice Production — Ingo R. Titze — The reference on how the folds vibrate and how airflow drives them; the source for the myoelastic-aerodynamic view this book leans on.
  • Practical Vocal Acoustics — Kenneth Bozeman — Turns formant theory into studio decisions about vowels and resonance, especially at the top of the range.
  • Your Voice: An Inside View — Scott McCoy — A clear bridge between voice science and pedagogy, written for singers and teachers rather than engineers.

Pedagogy & method

  • The Structure of Singing — Richard Miller — The core text behind much modern classical teaching; strongest on appoggio, registration, and vowel definition.
  • Solutions for Singers — Richard Miller — A question-and-answer format that addresses the exact problems singers bring to a teacher.
  • Complete Vocal Technique — Cathrine Sadolin — The book behind the CVT method; useful for its modes and for treating distortion as a controllable effect rather than damage.
  • The Functional Unity of the Singing Voice — Barbara Doscher — A widely used pedagogy text that links anatomy to day-to-day teaching choices.
  • Singing: The Mechanism and the Technic — William Vennard — A classic that later method books build on; still worth reading for the mechanism itself.
  • Bel Canto: A History of Vocal Pedagogy — James Stark — A scholarly history of the bel canto tradition and what its teachers actually taught.
  • Dynamics of the Singing Voice — Meribeth Bunch Dayme — A body-aware introduction to how the voice works and how to keep it working.

Performance, stage and health

  • Freeing the Natural Voice — Kristin Linklater — A foundational text on releasing habitual tension — the "tension release" half of singing.
  • The Actor Speaks — Patsy Rodenburg — Breath, presence, and voice on stage; read it for how performance nerves change the instrument.
  • Voice and the Actor — Cicely Berry — Text, breath, and speech for performance; the acting-side complement to singing technique.
  • The Voice Book — Kate DeVore and Starr Cookman — A practical, non-clinical guide to vocal health habits you can act on today.
  • Professional Voice: The Science and Art of Clinical Care — Robert T. Sataloff (editor) — The clinical reference on voice care, injury, and the professional voice user; heavy, but the place to go beyond the stop rule.

Reference & organizations

  • Journal of Voice — Peer-reviewed research on voice science, medicine, and pedagogy; where the evidence behind the claims lives.
  • Journal of Singing — The official journal of NATS; practical articles for teachers and singers bring the science into the studio.
  • NATS (National Association of Teachers of Singing) — nats.org — The professional association for singing teachers, with a teacher directory and the Journal of Singing.
  • The Voice Foundation — voicefoundation.org — A nonprofit for voice science and care; home of the annual symposium and the Journal of Voice.
  • VASTA (Voice and Speech Trainers Association) — voice and speech training for the stage, with resources for the actor-singer.
  • Pan American Vocology Association (PAVA) — A home for the science and practice of voice training and habilitation.
